extracted.intended_audience: owners/operators of stationary combustion turbines, facility environmental compliance staff, equipment manufacturers, environmental consultants, and regulatory attorneys
extracted.subtask_description: Preamble and final rule guidance for applicability, subcategorization, and standards-of-performance (BSER) determination for new and reconstructed stationary combustion turbines under 40 CFR part 60, subpart TTTTa. Covers exemptions, CHP treatment, fuel/type adjustments, calculation bases (HHV vs LHV, gross vs net), and fixed electric-sales thresholds for low/intermediate/base load subcategories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability exemptions (specified unit types)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain combustion turbines are excluded from some requirements: (1) units capable of deriving >=50% heat input from non-fossil fuel at base load and limited to <=10% annual fossil fuel capacity factor; (2) combined heat and power (CHP) units with federally enforceable permit limiting annual net electric sales to <=219,000 MWh or design_efficiency*potential_output, whichever greater; (3) units serving a generator along with other steam generating units, IGCC, or stationary combustion turbines where effective generation capacity is <=25 MW; (4) municipal waste combustors subject to 40 CFR part 60, subpart Eb; (5) commercial/industrial solid waste incineration units subject to 40 CFR part 60, subpart CCCC; (6) units deriving >50% heat input from an industrial process that produces no electrical/mechanical output used outside the affected turbine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These specific categories were listed as not subject to some proposed requirements; treat each exemption as tied to a federally enforceable permit condition or to specific regulatory subparts. Check unit-specific facts (fuel share, host facility arrangements, capacity) against the listed exemption criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability in non-continental and non-contiguous areas
rubrics_metrics.description: For non-continental (Hawaii, Virgin Islands, Guam, American Samoa, Puerto Rico, Northern Mariana Islands) and non-contiguous areas (those plus Alaska), only the initial BSER component will apply to combustion turbines; CCS-based numerical standards in 2032 will not apply to base load combustion turbines in these areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA considered regional unit deployment and concluded limited impact; Agency retains authority to amend in future rulemakings. Owners/operators in these areas should expect only the initial (non-CCS) BSER to apply under this final action.

rubrics_metrics.name: CHP net electric sales calculation and restriction on subtracting host purchased power
rubrics_metrics.description: For CHP units, net electric sales and net energy output are calculated similarly to non-CHP EGUs; the prior 20% minimum electrical output restriction (to use CHP-specific method) is eliminated for subpart TTTTa. Third-party CHP developers may subtract only the portion of host purchased power proportional to the percentage of useful thermal output provided by that specific CHP unit when determining net electric sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prevents multiple third-party developers serving the same host from each subtracting the host's entire purchased power (double counting) and prevents trivial thermal output to many hosts to game applicability. Purchased power of the host facility must be determined based on the percentage of thermal power provided by the specific CHP facility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-natural-gas stationary combustion turbine treatment (exemption removed)
rubrics_metrics.description: The prior exemption for turbines not physically capable of combusting natural gas (e.g., not connected to a gas pipeline) is not included in subpart TTTTa; such turbines, when burning fuels with higher heat-input emission rates than natural gas, adjust the natural-gas-fired emissions rate by the ratio of the heat-input-based emission rates and must maintain the same efficiency standard as a natural gas-fired turbine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Owners/operators burning non-natural-gas fuels must still meet a standard of performance based on the identified BSER, with emission-rate adjustments made on a lb CO2/MMBtu heat-input basis to account for higher-emitting fuels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three subcategories by electric sales: low, intermediate, base load
rubrics_metrics.description: Subpart TTTTa finalizes three subcategories—low load, intermediate load, and base load combustion turbines—determined based on electric sales (percent of potential electric output) on both a 12-operating month and 3-year rolling average basis. The applicable subcategory is determined each operating month and units may switch subcategories if operations change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Electric sales (capacity factor) is used as a proxy for operational profile (starts/stops, steady-state hours) and for determining the appropriate BSER and emission standards for a unit. Subcategorization is applied monthly and can change as operational patterns change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of electric sales (percent) as proxy for operation and BSER determination
rubrics_metrics.description: Electric sales relative to potential output reflects operational limitations inherent in unit design and indicates which emission-reduction technologies are suitable; for example, low-load turbines have frequent starts/stops and variable emissions, making certain output-based standards or CCS impracticable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating BSER or setting standards, consider how percent electric sales correlates with starts/stops, hours-per-start, and suitability of controls (efficiency measures vs CCS). EPA used industry operation data to justify subcategorization by electric sales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basis for design efficiency calculation: higher heating value (HHV)
rubrics_metrics.description: Design efficiency for potential electric output and electric-sales threshold calculation is based on the higher heating value (HHV) of fuel rather than the lower heating value (LHV). HHV is larger than LHV (approx. 10% higher for pipeline natural gas), so using HHV lowers the calculated potential electric output and thus lowers the electric sales threshold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure all efficiency comparisons use the same heating-value basis (HHV vs LHV). Although manufacturers often express turbine efficiency on an LHV basis, EPA references technologies on an HHV basis and will compute heat input on HHV for design-efficiency purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gross vs net electric output basis and optional net-equivalent standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Most EPA output-based standards are finalized based on gross electric output. EPA is including optional equivalent standards on a net-output basis to recognize minimizing auxiliary/parasitic loads; EPA used conversion assumptions of a 2% auxiliary load for simple and combined cycle turbines and a 7% auxiliary load for combined cycle EGUs using 90% CCS when converting to net output.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If applying net-output standards, use the specified auxiliary-load conversion factors. Document whether gross or net basis is used and ensure consistent basis across comparisons and compliance calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elimination of 50%/33% design-efficiency caps and sliding-scale threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: Subpart TTTTa removes the prior 50% maximum and 33% minimum restrictions on design efficiency used to calculate electric-sales thresholds and eliminates the sliding-scale threshold based on design efficiency. Instead, EPA is finalizing fixed percent electric-sales thresholds; design efficiency no longer alters the subcategorization thresholds (though design efficiency still figures into potential electric output calculation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Removing the caps preserves incentives for manufacturers to develop higher-efficiency turbines. When determining subcategory applicability, apply the fixed thresholds rather than scaling by (capped) design efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixed intermediate-to-base load electric-sales threshold: 40 percent
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA is finalizing a fixed electric-sales (capacity factor) threshold of 40% between intermediate load and base load combustion turbines. Units with 12-operating month electric sales >=40% (and 3-year rolling average criteria) are base load and subject to more stringent BSER (e.g., combined-cycle/CCS options); those below are intermediate or low load.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 40% reflects the point where adding HRSG/combined-cycle becomes economical and where combined-cycle EGUs maintain consistent emission rates. Using 40% also aligns BSER determination (CCS practicability) and cost-effectiveness analyses (LCOE comparisons accounting for economies of scale and variable operation).

rubrics_metrics.name: BSER for intermediate-load combustion turbines: efficient design and operation (not CCS)
rubrics_metrics.description: For intermediate-load turbines (generally simple cycle units that start/stop frequently and vary load), EPA determined efficient design and operation is the BSER because CCS is not practicable due to lack of a HRSG and frequent cycling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Owners/operators of intermediate-load turbines should focus on design and operational efficiency measures rather than CCS installation; applicability depends on operational profile and unit configuration.

rubrics_metrics.name: BSER for base-load combustion turbines: combined cycle and CCS practicability
rubrics_metrics.description: For base-load combustion turbines (units operating at relatively high loads with fewer starts/stops), EPA found CCS practicable and appropriate as part of BSER assessment; combined cycle generation is the first BSER component for base-load units and CCS is more effective on units running at base-load levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For units exceeding the 40% threshold, evaluate combined-cycle configurations and CCS feasibility as part of compliance planning; EPA based final standards on emissions performance of recently installed combined-cycle turbines with >=40% 12-operating month capacity factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Low-load subcategory characterization and threshold evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Low-load (peaking) turbines operate only during peak demand and provide ramping/ancillary services; highly variable operation produces variable and higher emissions rates, making reasonable output-based standards difficult. EPA evaluated electric-sales thresholds of 10%, 15%, 20%, and 25% and concluded 10% is problematic because emission rates are highly variable and most recent turbines do not operate below 10% capacity factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA observed that GHG emission rates begin to stabilize above 15% capacity factor; therefore, when setting the low/intermediate cutpoint consider that units with >15% capacity factor have more stable emission performance. Regulators should avoid thresholds (like 10%) that would capture many turbines with variable/unstable emission rates and create infeasible compliance obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monthly and rolling-average determination of subcategory applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: Subcategory determination is made each operating month based on percent electric sales on both a 12-operating month and a 3-year rolling average basis; a turbine can switch subcategories month-to-month if operations change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Owners/operators must track monthly electric sales and rolling-average metrics to determine subcategory and applicable standard in each month; plan for potential switching and how compliance will be demonstrated during transitions.
